messages.text:
Poseidon, one of the twelve Olympian deities in Greek mythology, is known as the god of the sea, storms, earthquakes, and horses. His domain is vast, encompassing all bodies of water, and he plays a crucial role in the balance of the natural world. Often depicted with a trident, his symbol of power, Poseidon could summon storms and earthquakes, earning him the title "Earth-Shaker."

Poseidon is the brother of Zeus, king of the gods, and Hades, god of the underworld. After the Olympians defeated the Titans, the three brothers divided the cosmos. Zeus claimed the sky, Hades took the underworld, and Poseidon ruled over the sea. Despite his dominion, Poseidon had a volatile and unpredictable nature, often reflecting the tumultuous and ever-changing ocean he controlled.

He was also known for his many romantic escapades and offspring, much like his brother Zeus. One of his most famous children is the hero Theseus. However, his relationships with mortals and other gods were not always smooth; for instance, Poseidon held a grudge against Odysseus after the hero blinded his son, the Cyclops Polyphemus, leading to the long and arduous journey home described in **The Odyssey**.

Poseidon’s temperament and domain made him both revered and feared by sailors and coastal communities. People would often offer sacrifices to appease him and ensure safe voyages or calm waters.

In addition to the sea, Poseidon was also associated with horses. He is said to have created the first horse and was often worshipped in connection with horse racing and other equestrian activities. Temples and sanctuaries dedicated to Poseidon could often be found near bodies of water or in cities with a strong connection to the sea, like Corinth.
